newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bolivia sees debt relief decision by June, July.
newsitem.headline: Bolivia sees debt relief decision by June, July.

text.p: Bolivia expects a decision by June or July on whether it will be one of the first countries to benefit from a new international initiative to ease debt loads of poor nations, its finance minister said on Friday.
The decision on helping Bolivia, one of Latin America's poorest countries, could "probably come by June or maybe July," Fernando Candia told a news conference.
The move would cover $200 to $700 million of Bolivia's total $4.6 billion external debt, said Candia, who was in Paris to attend an international donors' meeting on Bolivia hosted by the World Bank.
He said that the size of the debt relief was still being discussed but that it should involve an amount in the middle of the $200 million to $700 million range.

IMF head Michel Camdessus said earlier this week he expected Uganda, Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso and Bolivia to be among the first wave of countries to benefit from the debt plan agreed last year by the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Paris Club of creditor nations.
The programme is aimed at cutting the debt of heavily indebted countries to a sustainable level, allowing them to focus their energies on implementing economic reforms.
"Bolivia has an outstanding record (in economic reform) and so we consider it has a very strong case for favourable consideration," said Paul Isenman, World Bank country director.
The enhanced debt relief plan is due to be discussed at the twice-yearly meeting of the IMF and World Bank in Washington later this month.

Candia said the money freed from servicing Bolivia's debt would be spent in such areas as health and education and could boost Bolivia's annual GDP growth, now running at four percent, by as much as one percentage point.
Bolivia has taken big steps to modernise its economy, privatise public enterprises and cut inflation. But education levels remain low and health conditions rank among the worst in the continent.
International donors at the World Bank meeting agreed to a record disbursement of $800 million of already committed aid.

They pledged a further $650 million in new aid but said its disbursement would depend on whichever party winning Bolivia's June national elections pursued the country's ambitious economic reform programme.
"The new commitments would depend very much on the politics and programmes of the new government," said Isenman.
Jose Guilermo Justiniano, Minister of the Presidency, told the news conference he believed Bolivia's reform programme was irreversible.
"The reforms have too much popular support," Justiniano said. "I believe whichever party takes power, the political reforms will be preserved."
